newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: President quits warring Brazzaville to fete Kabila.
newsitem.headline: President quits warring Brazzaville to fete Kabila.

text.p: Congo's President Pascal Lissouba left his capital Brazzaville on Monday for the first time since a civil war broke out three weeks ago, flying over for national day festivities in Laurent Kabila's "other" Congo.

A spokesman said Lissouba took a short flight to the twin capital of Kinshasa across the Congo river, a sign his government forces are in full control of Brazzaville airport over which a heavy battle was fought last week.

Brazzaville was relatively calm on Monday, the third day of a new ceasefire between Lissouba and former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso, after a bout of mysterious shelling in the middle of the night.

"It woke me up at about three o'clock. We've got no idea who was firing. I did see some tracer fire but I've got no idea where it came from," one expatriate still in the capital told Reuters by telephone.
Lissouba was due to return home in the evening after the Independence Day celebrations in the former Zaire, the first since Kabila ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko in May.

French ambassador Raymond Cesaire, the only foreign envoy left in the capital of Lissouba's oil-rich central African country, said there was still some isolated shooting around his embassy on Monday but very little compared with previous days.

Fighting and hostile government troops had trapped Cesaire for days in the city-centre embassy, just 200 metres (yards) from the front line, but he managed on Sunday to move freely again, briefly visiting his residence in a safer part of town.

The former colonial city, wartime capital for "Free French" leader General Charles de Gaulle, has been devastated by shelling, street battles and thorough looting by soldiers since the bloody civil war erupted on June 5.
Aid workers estimate some 1,000 to 3,000 people, mostly civilians, have died in a conflict that has wavered between merciless artillery duels and truces that bring only relative and partial calm.
A lasting political solution seems no nearer.

Both Lissouba and Sassou say they want free and fair presidential elections, originally due on July 27 but put off by the fighting which began when the president tried to disarm his rival's powerful Cobra militia.
Lissouba claims Sassou has staged a coup attempt, while Sassou says Lissouba provoked the crisis as a pretext for extending his term in office that was to have ended next month.

Sassou's Radio Congo Freedom said that planeloads of Serb, Liberian and Angolan opposition UNITA mercenaries were flooding the Atlantic port of Pointe Noire, on their way to help Lissouba in the capital.

International mediation efforts led by Omar Bongo, president of neighbouring Gabon, have centred on the dispatch of an African intervention force but the United Nations says there must be a lasting peace first.
